The must-sees

  • Amsterdam Central Station

    Station · 1889

    Pierre Cuypers and A. L. van Gendt designed it, and it opened in 1889. It stands on artificial islands and cut the city off from its old harbour view.

    Look for: Compare the two towers. One clock face tells the time; the dial on the other shows which way the wind is blowing.

  • Anne Frank House

    Museum · 1960

    Anne Frank, her family and four others hid in the rear annex from 1942 until they were arrested in August 1944. Anne died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945; her diary was kept by Miep Gies, one of their helpers.

    Look for: Look up at the Westertoren next door. Anne wrote in her diary about hearing its clock chime from the hiding place.

  • Begijnhof

    Neighbourhood

    It was founded in the 14th century as a home for the Beguines, lay Catholic women who lived like nuns without taking vows. Het Houten Huis here is one of only two wooden houses left in the city centre.

    Look for: Opposite the English Church, the Catholic chapel hides behind ordinary house fronts. It was built in secret when Catholic worship was banned.

  • Canal Ring

    Neighbourhood

    The Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht were dug in the 17th century as a planned expansion for wealthy merchants. The canal ring became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

    Look for: Compare the gables along the top: step, neck and bell shapes, many with a hoisting beam sticking out for lifting goods through the windows.

  • Dam Square

    Square

    Amsterdam began with a dam built across the Amstel here, which gave the city its name. It has been the scene of markets, celebrations and protests for centuries.

    Look for: Behind the white National Monument, urns hold earth from execution sites and war cemeteries across the Netherlands and in Indonesia.

  • Rijksmuseum

    Museum · 1885

    Pierre Cuypers designed the building, which opened in 1885. Rembrandt’s Night Watch hangs in the gallery of honour at the heart of it.

  • Royal Palace

    Palace

    Jacob van Campen designed it as the city hall during the Golden Age, starting in 1648. Louis Napoleon turned it into a royal palace in 1808, and the king still uses it for state occasions.

    Look for: On top of the back facade, a bronze Atlas carries the globe on his shoulders.

  • Van Gogh Museum

    Museum · 1973

    The main building was designed by Gerrit Rietveld and opened in 1973, after his death. Much of the collection came from the painter’s brother Theo and his family.

    Look for: Behind the main building, find the low oval exhibition wing designed by the Japanese architect Kisho Kurokawa, opened in 1999.

  • Vondelpark

    Park · 1865

    It opened in 1865 as a park for horse riding and walking. It is named after the 17th-century poet Joost van den Vondel, whose statue stands inside.

    Look for: Near the middle of the park stands a concrete sculpture by Picasso, given to the city for the park’s centenary in 1965.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Amsterdam and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Amsterdam passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
